notes:
MORALITY AND CHANGE - CHAPTER OVERVIEW
- Opening quote: "Perhaps the most basic experience of human life is that it is a constant process of change." (Sean Fagan SM)
- Big question of the chapter: does morality (ethics) change with the times? Are some actions that were right in the past wrong now?
- The chapter looks at how society changes, how ways of thinking changed (the Enlightenment), and then uses two case studies to show how moral teaching developed: war and capital punishment. It ends with other examples of change: slavery, child labour and the rights of women.

THE TIMES THEY ARE A CHANGING
- George Best is seen by some as the cultural icon of the 1960s; maybe David Beckham will be seen as the icon of the 2000s.
- The chapter asks us to compare Ireland in the 60s/70s with the 90s/00s under these headings: fashion, music, religion, leisure, work, family, technology, money, travel, communication.
- These areas reflect our culture, and culture expresses our values.
- A lot of change takes place, yet certain truths remain the same always.

DEALING WITH CHANGE: DOES ETHICS CHANGE?
- Circumstances change radically over the centuries.
- Morality is about people. Virtues and vices within people stay the same.
- Pride, deceit and greed will always diminish a person in any age.
- Truth, love and selflessness will always be valued.
- But the world has changed hugely. New issues: cloning, weapons of mass destruction, the Internet (positive possibilities, but it also widens the availability of child pornography).
- These developments bring new moral questions, so ethics must develop to keep up with changes in society and answer the new questions.
- People's way of thinking also changes: new ideas about what it means to be human, happy and fulfilled. The way people work out moral questions can change too.

THE ENLIGHTENMENT: THE MODERN AGE
- Historians see the Enlightenment as a significant turning point and the beginning of the modern age.
- It generally refers to the eighteenth century and the time of the French Revolution.
- Dominant thinkers: philosophers, scientists and political theorists.
- Definition: The Enlightenment was a period when a break was made with ancient and medieval thought, in favour of a new trust in human reason and science.
- It challenged all sources of authority, including faith and the Church. The emphasis was solely on reason, which would replace faith as the guiding principle in everything.
- In the nineteenth century the movement was often deplored, especially by the Catholic Church, because it was seen as an attack on Christianity.
- The Church also criticised the rise of individualism and the distrust of authority and tradition that the Enlightenment brought.
- BUT ideas that began with the Enlightenment, such as democratic government and human rights, are now accepted by all, including the churches.
- Post-modernism: a more recent train of thought that attacks many tenets of the Enlightenment. It says reason alone cannot give us the whole truth about ourselves.

NEW SCIENCES, NEW EXPERIENCES, NEW LEARNING
- New human sciences teach us more about the person and how we know good and evil:
- socially (sociology)
- scientifically (science)
- psychologically (psychology)
- All this helps to shape and develop our ethics.
- We also learn from history. Example: the Holocaust, when six million Jews were exterminated, profoundly affected how people understood the effects of racism and the dangers of ethnic cleansing.
- Two issues used to show how moral thought has developed: the morality of war and the morality of capital punishment.

WAR AND PEACE
- War has always been part of human history.
- Some argue a 'high tech' war, such as Iraq in 2003, limits civilian casualties. But wars are very common, often very brutal and have many victims.

EYEWITNESS: A SURVIVOR'S STORY (RWANDA)
- The Kamuhandas were an ordinary Rwandan family. The trouble began when the aircraft carrying President Juvenal Habyarimana and his Burundian counterpart Cyprien Ntayamira was shot down.
- Hamis Kamuhanda was eleven at the time (eighteen when telling the story).
- Rumours spread that Hutus were out to kill every Tutsi, claiming Tutsis had killed the Hutu president.
- The family played dead; Hamis lost half of his right leg to a machete. Men had dragged his father out by his legs; he was never seen again.
- The armed Hutu men were called the Interahamwe.
- They were liberated by RPF (Rwanda Patriotic Front) soldiers. Hamis spent about six months in hospital.
- He lost his father, his leg, his dignity, his education and his trust in his Hutu neighbours.
- He bore no grudges: "Hatred does not solve anything." Holding a grudge "would make me the same as them".
- He guards cars for tourists to earn money. He dreams, with a friend who also lost a leg, of setting up an athletics team to represent Rwanda at the Paralympics.
- Point of the story: the effects of war on ordinary people stay the same despite new technologies.

WAR IN SCRIPTURE AND THE EARLY CHURCH
- No evidence of Christians in the Roman army until 180 CE.
- Early Christians tended not to get involved in social institutions because they believed in the imminent return of Jesus (the Second Coming). Many quit jobs and withdrew from the world.
- When Jesus did not return immediately, Christians realised they must take part in the social structures around them.
- Christians saw themselves as basically pacifist (though they would not have used the word).
- Origen, a Father of the Church, taught: "Christians do not go forth as soldiers."
- The love command of Jesus seemed to rule out shedding blood.
- The Roman Empire looked on Christians with suspicion and questioned their loyalty.
- Two big changes:
- 1. Emperor Constantine made Christianity the official religion of the empire, so Christians became fully part of society.
- 2. The growing threat from the Barbarians: defending the empire and their way of life made it harder for Christians not to join the army.

JUSTIFICATION FOR WAR - AUGUSTINE
- Augustine was an African bishop, very familiar with the empire, and an important Christian writer.
- He believed order and the empire were preferable to chaos.
- In The City of God (Book 19, Chapter 17): "A just war, moreover, is justified only by the injustice of the aggressor, and that injustice ought to be a source of grief to any good man, because it is human injustice."
- In other words: peace is the ideal, but we should try to restrain war, which is inevitable.

JUSTIFICATION FOR WAR - AQUINAS
- Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologica) set three conditions before declaring a just war:
- 1. The authority of the sovereign by whose command the war is waged.
- 2. The hostility should begin because of some crime of the enemy.
- 3. A rightful intention: the advancement of good or the avoidance of evil.
- With Augustine he condemned within war: the passion for inflicting harm, the cruel thirst for vengeance, a plundering and implacable spirit, the fever of turmoil, the lust for power.
- Bishops and clerics were not to get involved in war. The ideal of pacifism remained.
- So the Church moved from non-involvement and pacifism to a theory that allowed war to defend one's society, as long as you acted justly within the war.
- This was reinforced by a growing sense that obedience to the State is a moral duty to God.
- The Truce of God: a practical Church initiative to limit fighting. No fighting from Wednesday vespers to Monday sunrise. Other versions banned fighting during Lent or Advent.

FRANCISCO SUAREZ - CLASSIC JUST WAR THEORY
- The classic formulation of the Just War theory came from Francisco Suarez.
- Two parts: jus ad bellum (the justification for going to war) and jus in bello (the proper conduct of war).
- First, it must be waged by a legitimate power.
- Second, its cause must be just and right.
- Third, just methods must be used: equity at the beginning of war, in carrying it on, and in victory.
- "War in itself is not an evil, but it is often wrongly done."

JUST WAR THEORY AND PACIFISM
- Pacifism: the belief that no circumstances can make a war honest; it is evil in itself to go to war.
- Pacifist movements in society and in all Christian churches have become more powerful and vocal.
- The churches are not entirely pacifist, but a strong pacifist tradition remains in them.
- Pacifist reformed churches hold that Christianity is, of its essence, a pacifist faith. Examples: Waldensians, Mennonites, Quakers.
- Mennonites grew out of the Protestant Reformation; they believe the Lord's command to love one's enemies means they can never take part in the military.
- Quakers (the Religious Society of Friends) believe the Spirit of Christ would never move a person to fight and make war for the Kingdom of Christ or the kingdoms of this world.

POPES, WAR AND PEACE
- In the war-torn early to mid twentieth century, papal teaching focused on peace based on justice and charity.
- Pope Benedict XV placed the virtue of charity above the principles of a just war.
- Pope Pius XII (Christmas Message, 1944) declared wars of aggression immoral, while teaching the right to defence.
- Pacem in Terris (1963), Pope John XXIII: written at the height of the nuclear arms race between the Soviet Union and the USA. It seriously challenged the morality of nuclear war. States should relate in truth and justice and work for the international common good. The arms race works against truth and justice, spends resources on destruction, and holds back social and economic progress.

WAR IN THE MODERN ERA
- Can any modern war be justified, given weapons of mass destruction?
- For a Christian following biblical ethics, war reverses the Beatitudes: instead of visiting the sick we increase their number; instead of feeding the hungry we take away their means of production.
- War destroys not only life but all that makes us human: our values and our humanity.
- There is a serious critique of the Just War theory today, inside and outside the Christian community.
- Jus ad bellum questions: who is the proper authority? In the second Gulf War the USA went to war without clear approval of the United Nations. Is a revolution against an unjust oppressor ever justified if only a state can declare war?
- Jus in bello questions: can a modern war be fought without immoral acts? Many believe it is impossible, as innocent people will suffer and die - "war is hell".

PACIFISM AND NON-VIOLENCE
- Huge anti-war demonstrations worldwide before the Second Gulf War in 2003 suggest more people are against the use of force.
- Pope John Paul II was highly critical of the recent Gulf Wars in Iraq and strongly supported dialogue.
- Pax Christi is an exclusively pacifist movement.
- Mahatma Gandhi (1868-1948): his non-violent philosophy had a profound influence on modern thought.
- Satyagraha: means 'truth force'; peaceful, passive resistance to what is unjust; it has religious roots.
- Gandhi: "Satyagraha is a weapon of the strong. It admits of no violence under any circumstance whatever; and it always insists on the truth."
- The goal is to convert opponents, not kill them: "The essence of non-violent technique is that it seeks to liquidate antagonisms but not the antagonist."
- Current Catholic teaching: CCC Peace 2302-6; Avoiding War 2309-17. The Church still contains the Just War theory but has moved significantly toward (not completely embracing) pacifism.
- Biblical calls for peace: "Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God" (Matthew 5:9). "They shall beat their swords into ploughshares, and their spears into pruning hooks" (Isaiah 2:4).
- But teaching has always been open to a justifiable use of force. Pope John Paul II: peoples have "a right and even a duty to protect their existence and freedom by proportionate means against an unjust aggressor".
- John Paul II, 1982 Day of Peace: because nuclear or bacteriological war differs in nature from classical war, and because of the scandal of the arms race against the needs of the Third World, the right to defence underlines the urgency for the world to develop effective means of negotiation.
- Joan D. Chittister OSB, Modern Prayer for World Peace: "vengeance begets violence".
- Exercise: apply the theory to the 2003 Gulf War in Iraq (US and UK coalition to oust Saddam Hussein and destroy the threat of weapons of mass destruction).

CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
- Capital punishment: the death penalty; the State executing people who have committed very serious crimes.
- Oscar Wilde, The Ballad of Reading Gaol: "There is no chapel on the day on which they hang a man..."
- One of the most emotive issues in public life; it divides opinion across the globe.

CASE STUDY: PAUL HILL
- Paul Hill, aged forty-nine, executed by lethal injection in northern Florida (2003) for murdering two people outside an abortion clinic in 1994.
- He killed Dr John Britton and his driver James Barrett outside the Ladies Center in Pensacola, Florida. He gave himself up, saying he killed to prevent 'innocent babies' being killed.
- Florida Governor Jeb Bush (brother of President George W. Bush) could have commuted the sentence to life imprisonment but said he would not be 'bullied' into stopping it.
- Former Presbyterian minister; about 100 demonstrators hailed him as a martyr. He was unrepentant: said he would kill again and that the state "will be making me a martyr".
- The execution was criticised by an unusual alliance: anti-abortion Christian protesters and anti-death penalty activists.
- Floridians for Alternatives to the Death Penalty wrote to Jeb Bush asking him to commute the sentence, saying "killing Paul Hill will actually encourage more murder".

CHRISTIAN TEACHING FOR CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
- Christ himself was executed by the Roman state under orders of the Governor of Judea. Many Christians have been executed for their faith (martyrs).
- Yet Christian ethics has not always opposed the death penalty; there is an argument in favour.
- Genesis 9:6: "Whoever sheds the blood of a human, by a human shall that person's blood be shed; for in his own image God made humankind."
- In the Law of Moses, fifteen different crimes carried the death penalty.
- 'Thou shalt not kill' is read as 'thou shalt not murder or take innocent life'.
- Self-defence is generally accepted. The State's right to execute those who threaten the common good is seen as an extension of the right to protect oneself.
- Romans 13: the ruler "does not bear the sword in vain; he is the servant of God to execute his wrath on the wrongdoer" (Romans 13:1-7; 1 Peter 2:13-17).
- So it could be held to be the State's duty; the death penalty is an exercise in judgement, not hatred.
- Pope Innocent III: the State can exercise "a judgement of blood, without mortal sin", if it punishes "not in hate, but in judgement; not incautiously, but after consideration".
- Deterrence argument: if people know killing could lead to their own death, it should stop them killing; it contributes to public order.

CHRISTIAN TEACHING AGAINST CAPITAL PUNISHMENT
- Many Christians now hold it is entirely wrong for the State to execute people.
- Jesus did not encourage a 'quid pro quo' justice (if you cause a death you should die). He is gracious and forgiving toward the sinner.
- Gandhi: "an eye for an eye makes the whole world blind".
- CCC paragraph 2266 still allows the proper authority to protect the common good with punishment, including the death penalty in grave situations.
- Pope John Paul II, Evangelium vitae (The Gospel of Life), paragraph 56, goes further than the CCC. The letter defends the dignity of life. He notes the growing desire to abolish the death penalty. The only justification would be if there were no other way to protect society; today such cases are rare, if not non-existent.
- Clear movement in teaching: human dignity always stays with the person no matter what they do; society never has the right to take their life.
- Deterrence: the death penalty has not been shown to reduce violent crime, so it has no real significance as a deterrent.
- Retribution: in July 1976 the US Supreme Court said capital punishment was not cruel or unusual punishment; it did not work as a deterrent but was a form of retribution. For Christians, death as punishment seems against a gospel ethic of life for all.
- Other issues: an innocent person executed cannot be corrected; in the USA a disproportionate number of people from minority ethnic groups are on 'death row'.
- Key questions: can the State justifiably kill? Does someone forfeit the right to live by their actions?

CHANGE AND SOCIETY - OTHER AREAS
- Slavery: part of life in biblical times and seemed acceptable to New Testament writers. Thomas Jefferson, writer of the American Constitution (as the book says), had African American slaves. Only in the last two centuries did slavery become illegal and widely seen as against human dignity. Modern forms: child labour in factories, abuse of people in prostitution, illegal trafficking of refugees, child soldiers.
- Child labour: long accepted in the world economy; now more awareness of exploitation of children as cheap labour. Example: Iris, a teenager who works full time gathering coffee beans on the Santa Marta coffee plantation in northern Nicaragua. (Trocaire Lenten Campaign 2002.)
- Rights of women: women's right to take part in democracy was very limited until the last two centuries. This reflects a patriarchal society - one where all power was held by men and opportunities for women were severely restricted. Perhaps no area of change has been more necessary and profound.
- Growing understanding of the dignity of the individual: greater respect for rights of workers, children and women. Out of this awareness ethics changes, grows and develops.
- Values also change, and not always for good: the new economy brought opportunities but also more individualism, greed and loss of community.
- Morality never takes place in a vacuum; there is always a context that shapes it.
- There is also a constancy in ethics: ethics cannot simply change along with society - it is the conscience of society as it changes and develops.

SUMMARY
- Change in society is a reality.
- Ethics develops over time because we know more about the person and the world through science, we learn from history, and new political and social contexts shape teaching.
- The teaching on war, capital punishment and slavery has developed and changed over the centuries.

KEY TERMS
- The Enlightenment: 18th-century break with ancient and medieval thought in favour of trust in human reason and science.
- Just war: a war that meets set conditions for going to war (jus ad bellum) and for fighting it (jus in bello).
- Pacifist movements: groups who hold that war is evil in itself and never justified.
- Capital punishment: the death penalty imposed by the State.
- Post-modernism: the view that reason alone cannot give the whole truth about ourselves.
- Satyagraha: Gandhi's 'truth force' - peaceful, passive resistance to injustice.
- Patriarchal society: a society where all power is held by men.

rows.prompt: Outline how Christian teaching on war developed from the early Church to the classic Just War theory. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: The early Christians were basically pacifist. Believing the Second Coming was imminent, they withdrew from society, and there is no evidence of Christians in the Roman army before 180 CE. Origen taught that 'Christians do not go forth as soldiers', and Jesus' love command seemed to rule out shedding blood. This changed when Constantine made Christianity the official religion of the empire, so Christians became part of society, and when the Barbarian threat made defence of the empire necessary. Augustine, an African bishop, argued in The City of God that a just war is 'justified only by the injustice of the aggressor': peace is the ideal, but war must be restrained. Aquinas, in the Summa Theologica, set three conditions: the authority of the sovereign, a cause based on a crime of the enemy, and a rightful intention. With Augustine he condemned vengeance, plunder and lust for power in war, and clerics were not to fight. The Church also tried to limit fighting through the Truce of God, banning fighting from Wednesday vespers to Monday sunrise. Finally Francisco Suarez gave the classic formulation, separating jus ad bellum (justification for war) from jus in bello (proper conduct): war must be waged by a legitimate power, for a just cause, using just methods. So teaching moved from pacifism to allowing war to defend society.

Award marks for accurate sequence of development.

rows.prompt: 'The Catholic Church has moved significantly toward pacifism but has not fully embraced it.' Discuss this statement. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Pacifism is the belief that no circumstances make a war honest; going to war is evil in itself. In the twentieth century papal teaching moved toward peace. Pope Benedict XV placed charity above the principles of a just war. Pope Pius XII in 1944 declared wars of aggression immoral. Pope John XXIII's Pacem in Terris (1963), written at the height of the nuclear arms race, challenged the morality of nuclear war and said the arms race works against truth and justice and wastes resources. Pope John Paul II strongly criticised the Gulf Wars in Iraq and promoted dialogue, and movements like Pax Christi are fully pacifist. Scripture supports this: 'Blessed are the peacemakers' (Matthew 5:9) and 'They shall beat their swords into ploughshares' (Isaiah 2:4). Many also argue war reverses the Beatitudes and that innocent people will always suffer. However, the Church has not fully embraced pacifism. The CCC (2309-17) still contains the Just War theory. John Paul II said peoples have 'a right and even a duty to protect their existence and freedom by proportionate means against an unjust aggressor', though in 1982 he stressed the urgency of negotiation because nuclear war is different in nature. By contrast, the Mennonites and Quakers hold that Christianity is of its essence pacifist. So the statement is accurate.

rows.prompt: Show how Christian teaching on capital punishment has developed and changed over time. (20 marks)
rows.model_answer: Traditionally Christians argued in favour of capital punishment. Genesis 9:6 says 'Whoever sheds the blood of a human, by a human shall that person's blood be shed', and the Law of Moses named fifteen crimes for the death penalty. 'Thou shalt not kill' was read as 'thou shalt not murder or take innocent life'. Self-defence was accepted, and the State's right to execute those who threaten the common good was seen as an extension of it. Romans 13 says the ruler 'does not bear the sword in vain'. Pope Innocent III taught the State may exercise 'a judgement of blood, without mortal sin' if it acts not in hate but in judgement. It was also seen as a deterrent. Today many Christians believe execution is entirely wrong. Jesus did not teach a 'quid pro quo' justice; he was forgiving to sinners, and as Gandhi said, 'an eye for an eye makes the whole world blind'. The CCC (2266) still allows the death penalty in grave situations, but John Paul II in Evangelium vitae (56) went further: the only justification is if there is no other way to protect society, which today is rare if not non-existent. Modern arguments add that it is not a proven deterrent, innocent people cannot be brought back, and minorities are over-represented on death row. Teaching has moved toward the view that human dignity can never be taken away.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. May refer to: Genesis 9:6; Law of Moses; reading of 'Thou shalt not kill'; self-defence/common good; Romans 13; Innocent III; deterrence; Jesus' forgiveness; Gandhi quote; CCC 2266; Evangelium vitae 56; deterrence not proven; innocent executed; minorities on death row; human dignity. Must show both the earlier and the modern position.

rows.prompt: Outline two reasons why ethics develops over time, giving an example of each from your study. (10 marks)
rows.model_answer: First, the world changes and brings new moral questions. Issues such as cloning, weapons of mass destruction and the Internet did not exist before, so ethics must develop to answer them. For example, modern weapons of mass destruction led Pope John XXIII in Pacem in Terris to challenge the morality of nuclear war. Second, we learn from history and from new human sciences. Sociology, science and psychology teach us more about the human person. The Holocaust, in which six million Jews were killed, deeply changed how people understood racism and ethnic cleansing. A growing understanding of human dignity has also changed teaching on slavery, child labour and the rights of women: slavery seemed acceptable in biblical times but is now seen as against human dignity.
rows.marking_scheme: Two reasons x 5 marks: reason stated 2 marks + explanation with example 3 marks. Possible reasons: new issues (cloning, WMD, Internet); new ways of thinking (Enlightenment); new human sciences (sociology, science, psychology); learning from history (Holocaust); growing awareness of dignity (slavery, women, child labour).
